analysis.title: Parsing the 13F reports
key_insights: Q3 2026 13F filings show continued differentiation in hedge fund long US equity positioning. Technology had the largest sector allocation increase but hedge funds remain substantially underweight the sector versus the S&P 500. Industry AUM was about USD 3.8 trillion at quarter end.
The 13F filings exclude short positions and are published with a delay, so they are a backward-looking snapshot of long holdings, not a real-time view of positioning.

Q3 context: July's sharp reversal in AI-linked stocks coincided with scrutiny of valuations, AI capex, funding needs and expected returns. Middle East conflict and energy disruption pushed oil, inflation concerns and yields higher. Tech recovered in August, then rotated lower in September on energy costs and yields.
The HFRX Global Hedge Fund Index fell 0.8% in Q3 versus a 2.0% gain for the S&P 500. Performance was concentrated in a narrow group of strategies.

Cryptocurrency strategies returned 25.6% in Q3 as Bitcoin gained about 44%. Commodity Hedge returned +7.2%, Activist +7.1% and CTAs +6.0%. Distressed Debt fell 7.1%, Fixed Income Arbitrage -1.2% and Equity L/S -0.6%.

Reported hedge fund long allocation to Tech rose 0.9 percentage points in Q3. Healthcare and Energy rose 0.3 points each, Communication Services and Financials 0.2 each. Industrials fell 0.8 points, Consumer Discretionary 0.5 and Materials 0.2.

The S&P 500 Information Technology index gained 7% in Q3, so part of the 0.9-point Tech weight increase reflects market performance rather than net purchases. The data do not show how much came from active buying.
Aggregate active weight versus the S&P 500 rose from 27.0% at end-2025 to 31.1% in Q1 and 33.6% in Q2, then eased to 32.3% in Q3. It remains close to its highest level since 2012.

Hedge fund Tech allocation is 22.4% versus a 39.7% S&P 500 weight, a 17.3 point underweight and the largest relative sector position in either direction. Healthcare is the largest overweight at 3.1 points, then Industrials 2.3, Materials 2.0 and Financials 1.6.

The Tech underweight has widened since 2022. Before 2022 the gap ranged from neutral to about 6 points below the S&P 500. Pictet reads it as a structural shift in the benchmark that hedge fund allocations have not matched, not an outright withdrawal from Tech.

Insider buyer-to-seller ratios moderated through end-September, but since then the S&P 500 ratio has kept declining while the Tech ratio shows a marked resurgence in insider buying in November alongside the sector's decline, consistent with past dip-buying.

The beta of the HFRX Global Hedge Fund Index to MSCI World peaked near 0.58 in early 2026, fell sharply and recovered only partially. It stayed below the peak through Q3 despite strong global equities.

Manager moves on Tech were mixed. Point72 added Microsoft, Celestica and Intel and cut Credo, ASML and TSMC. Citadel added Cloudflare and cut Nvidia and Microsoft. Renaissance added Micron and AMD and cut Palantir and TSMC. Several managers also reduced broad-market ETF holdings.

The top 25 reported hedge fund long holdings are led by Nvidia, Amazon and Microsoft, then SpaceX and Apple. Microsoft's market value rose 35% on a 37.5% price gain while the reported position fell 2%. Nvidia's market value rose 16% while its position rose 2%.

Among the top 25, Intel's position rose 83% and Meta's 11%. SanDisk fell 24%, AMD 15%, Micron 10% and Apple 9%. The iShares Core S&P 500 ETF position fell 47%, Vanguard S&P 500 ETF rose 38% and SPDR S&P 500 ETF rose 2%, which points to rotation between vehicles.

Largest position increases (holdings above USD 1B) were led by ETFs, including the ARK Innovation ETF and the Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF (+210%). Industrials featured: Honeywell Aerospace +158%, GFL Environmental +156%, Cummins and Curtiss-Wright +103%, Sunbelt Rentals +100%. Tech: NXP +116%, Shopify +89%, Intel +83%.

Largest position reductions (holdings above USD 1B): Medline -68%, iShares Core S&P 500 ETF -47%, Nebius -41%, Lockheed Martin -38%, Bloom Energy -37%, NetApp -37%, Republic Services -35%, Otis -34%, STMicroelectronics -34%, Qualcomm -33%, 3M -32%, Zoom -31%.
Most new positions by manager count: Medtronic and Meta each had seven initiators (about USD 3.7B and USD 2.7B). Intel had six managers initiating about USD 2.7B.

Most full exits by manager count: SpaceX six managers (about USD 2.4B), SPDR S&P 500 ETF four (USD 2.0B), Applied Materials four (USD 1.9B), Microsoft four (USD 1.2B). Microsoft was also newly added by five managers and SpaceX initiated by three, so the same names sit on both buy and sell screens.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech had the largest sector allocation increase in Q3 (+0.9 points), managers such as Point72 and Renaissance added names, and insiders are buying Tech again in November as the sector declines.
tension_points.bear_case: Hedge funds remain 17.3 points underweight Tech versus the S&P 500, part of the Q3 increase reflects the sector's 7% price gain, and other managers such as Citadel cut Nvidia and Microsoft while four exited Applied Materials fully.

theme_stances.key_argument: Technology remained central to Q3 portfolio activity, but the data show selective repositioning and substantial disagreement rather than a broad-based increase in exposure.
theme_stances.evidence: substantial disagreement and portfolio turnover beneath the aggregate data

theme_stances.key_argument: As Tech has come under pressure, sector insiders have started buying again, consistent with past dip-buying behaviour.
theme_stances.evidence: sector insiders have started buying again
